title: SBI Specialist (Systems) Promotion - MCQ Practice Bank

topics.topic: DR / BCP Framework in Banking Systems

questions.question: Which component of Linux directly manages the CPU, memory and hardware devices?

options.A: Window manager
options.B: Shell
options.C: Kernel
options.D: Terminal emulator

questions.answer_text: Kernel
questions.explanation: The kernel is the core of the OS; it schedules processes, manages memory and talks to device drivers.

questions.question: In Linux, the shell mainly acts as:

options.A: The boot loader that loads the kernel into memory at startup
options.B: A device driver that handles keyboard and screen input
options.C: A command interpreter between the user and the kernel
options.D: The core component that schedules processes and manages memory

questions.answer_text: A command interpreter between the user and the kernel
questions.explanation: The shell (bash, sh, ksh) reads user commands and asks the kernel to execute them.

questions.question: The Linux kernel is best described as:

options.A: Monolithic kernel with loadable modules
options.B: Hybrid kernel derived from Windows NT
options.C: Pure microkernel with drivers in user space
options.D: Exokernel with no hardware abstraction

questions.answer_text: Monolithic kernel with loadable modules
questions.explanation: Linux is monolithic (drivers run in kernel space) but supports loadable kernel modules (insmod/modprobe).

questions.question: When a user program needs to read a file, it switches from user mode to kernel mode through a:

options.A: Shell alias
options.B: Context switch only
options.C: Interrupt vector table
options.D: System call

questions.answer_text: System call
questions.explanation: System calls (read, write, open, fork) are the controlled entry point from user mode into kernel mode.

questions.question: Which directory holds system-wide configuration files in Linux?

options.A: /var
options.B: /opt
options.C: /etc
options.D: /bin

questions.answer_text: /etc
questions.explanation: /etc stores configuration files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/fstab, /etc/hosts.

questions.question: System and application log files are normally stored under:

options.A: /boot/log
options.B: /etc/log
options.C: /usr/log
options.D: /var/log

questions.answer_text: /var/log
questions.explanation: /var holds variable data; /var/log holds logs like messages, secure, syslog.

questions.question: Device files such as /dev/sda are located in which directory?

options.A: /home
options.B: /etc
options.C: /boot
options.D: /dev

questions.answer_text: /dev
questions.explanation: /dev contains special files that represent hardware devices.

questions.question: The /proc directory in Linux is:

options.A: A virtual file system exposing kernel and process information at runtime
options.B: A disk partition that stores compiled program binaries for all users
options.C: A hidden folder where deleted files are kept for recovery
options.D: A dedicated swap area used when physical memory is full

questions.answer_text: A virtual file system exposing kernel and process information at runtime
questions.explanation: /proc is generated in memory by the kernel, e.g. /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo, /proc/<PID>.

questions.question: Which structure stores a file's permissions, owner, size and data block pointers, but NOT its name?

options.A: Inode
options.B: Journal
options.C: Superblock
options.D: Boot block

questions.answer_text: Inode
questions.explanation: The inode holds metadata; the file name is stored in the directory entry that points to the inode.

questions.question: The superblock of a Linux file system contains:

options.A: The process table listing all running processes and their PIDs
options.B: Metadata of the whole file system such as size, block count and free blocks
options.C: Hashed user passwords along with account expiry information
options.D: The actual data blocks of all user files, along with their names and directory paths

questions.answer_text: Metadata of the whole file system such as size, block count and free blocks
questions.explanation: The superblock describes the file system itself; corruption of it makes the file system unmountable.

questions.question: Which statement about hard links and soft (symbolic) links is correct?

options.A: A soft link shares the same inode as the original file
options.B: Deleting the original file breaks a hard link
options.C: A hard link shares the same inode as the original file
options.D: Hard links can span different file systems

questions.answer_text: A hard link shares the same inode as the original file
questions.explanation: Hard links point to the same inode; a symlink has its own inode and stores a path, so it breaks if the target is deleted.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Linux-native file system?

options.A: NTFS
options.B: ext4
options.C: ext3
options.D: XFS

questions.answer_text: NTFS
questions.explanation: NTFS is the Windows file system; ext3, ext4 and XFS are Linux journaling file systems.

questions.question: Journaling in file systems like ext4 mainly helps to:

options.A: Defragment the disk automatically during idle periods
options.B: Compress files automatically when the disk is nearly full so that more data fits on it
options.C: Encrypt data at rest using a key stored in the superblock
options.D: Recover quickly and keep consistency after a crash by logging changes first

questions.answer_text: Recover quickly and keep consistency after a crash by logging changes first
questions.explanation: A journal records intended changes before they are committed, so a crash can be replayed or rolled back quickly.

questions.question: The file /etc/fstab is used to:

options.A: Store hashed user passwords and password aging details
options.B: Define file systems to be mounted automatically at boot
options.C: Configure firewall rules applied when the network starts
options.D: Schedule recurring jobs for all users of the system

questions.answer_text: Define file systems to be mounted automatically at boot
questions.explanation: /etc/fstab lists devices, mount points, file system types and mount options.

questions.question: After 'chmod 755 report.sh', the permissions are:

options.A: Owner rwx, group rwx, others r-x
options.B: Owner rw-, group r-x, others r-x
options.C: Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x
options.D: Owner rwx, group r--, others r--

questions.answer_text: Owner rwx, group r-x, others r-x

questions.question: What is the numeric (octal) form of the permission rw-r-----?
With umask 022, a newly created regular file gets which permissions by default?
questions.explanation: Files start from 666; 666 minus 022 gives 644 (rw-r--r--).

questions.question: With umask 027, a newly created directory gets which permissions?
questions.explanation: Directories start from 777; masking 027 gives 750 (rwxr-x---).

questions.question: Which command changes the owner of a file?

options.A: umask
options.B: chown
options.C: chmod
options.D: passwd

questions.answer_text: chown
questions.explanation: chown changes owner (and optionally group); chmod changes permissions.

questions.question: The sticky bit set on /tmp ensures that:

options.A: Files in it are hidden from all users except root
options.B: Only the file owner or root can delete or rename files in it
options.C: The directory becomes read-only for everyone except root
options.D: Every file in it runs with the privileges of its owner

questions.answer_text: Only the file owner or root can delete or rename files in it
questions.explanation: The sticky bit (t) on a shared directory prevents users from deleting each other's files.

questions.question: When the SUID bit is set on an executable, the program runs with the privileges of:

options.A: The file's owner
options.B: The group of the parent directory
options.C: The user who runs it
options.D: The root user always

questions.answer_text: The file's owner
questions.explanation: SUID makes the process run as the file owner, e.g. /usr/bin/passwd runs as root to update /etc/shadow.

questions.question: In 'ls -l' output, the permission string '-rwsr-xr-x' indicates:

options.A: Sticky bit is set
options.B: The file is a symbolic link
options.C: SUID bit is set
options.D: The file is a socket

questions.answer_text: SUID bit is set
questions.explanation: An 's' in the owner execute position means SUID is set and the owner has execute permission.

questions.question: In 'ls -l' output, a first character of 'd' means the entry is a:

options.A: Directory
options.B: Device file
options.C: Daemon
options.D: Deleted file

questions.answer_text: Directory
questions.explanation: First character: '-' regular file, 'd' directory, 'l' symlink, 'c'/'b' character/block device.

questions.question: Which command removes write permission for group and others?

options.A: chmod ug-w file
options.B: chmod o=w file
options.C: chmod a+w file
options.D: chmod go-w file

questions.answer_text: chmod go-w file
questions.explanation: g=group, o=others, '-w' removes write.

questions.question: setfacl and getfacl commands are used to:

options.A: Give permissions to specific users or groups beyond owner/group/others
options.B: Set disk usage quotas for individual users and groups on a mounted file system
options.C: Encrypt and decrypt individual files using each user's own key
options.D: Change the default umask applied to newly created files

questions.answer_text: Give permissions to specific users or groups beyond owner/group/others
questions.explanation: Access Control Lists allow finer control than the basic owner-group-others model.

questions.question: Which file stores user account details like username, UID, GID, home directory and login shell?

options.A: /etc/hosts
options.B: /etc/shadow
options.C: /etc/group
options.D: /etc/passwd

questions.answer_text: /etc/passwd
questions.explanation: /etc/passwd is world-readable and holds account info; hashed passwords are kept in /etc/shadow.

questions.question: Hashed user passwords are stored in:

options.A: /etc/passwd
options.B: /etc/shadow
options.C: /etc/profile
options.D: /etc/sudoers

questions.answer_text: /etc/shadow
questions.explanation: /etc/shadow is readable only by root and also holds password aging data.

questions.question: What is the UID of the root user?
questions.explanation: root always has UID 0; regular users usually start at 1000 (or 500 on older systems).

questions.question: Which command adds an existing user 'ravi' to the supplementary group 'dba' without removing him from other groups?

options.A: usermod -aG dba ravi
options.B: useradd -g dba ravi
options.C: usermod -G dba ravi
options.D: groupadd dba ravi

questions.answer_text: usermod -aG dba ravi
questions.explanation: -a (append) with -G keeps existing supplementary groups; -G alone replaces them.

questions.question: Which file controls which users may run commands as root using sudo?

options.A: /etc/passwd
options.B: /etc/sudoers
options.C: /etc/shadow
options.D: /etc/securetty

questions.answer_text: /etc/sudoers
questions.explanation: /etc/sudoers should be edited with 'visudo', which checks syntax before saving.

questions.question: Which command locks a user's password so that the user cannot log in with it?

options.A: chage -l username
options.B: userdel username
options.C: passwd -d username
options.D: passwd -l username

questions.answer_text: passwd -l username
questions.explanation: passwd -l (or usermod -L) locks the password; -d deletes it (dangerous - allows empty password).

questions.question: The 'chage' command is used to:

options.A: Change the login shell
options.B: Manage password aging and expiry
options.C: Change the home directory
options.D: Change a user's primary group

questions.answer_text: Manage password aging and expiry
questions.explanation: chage sets maximum/minimum password age, warning days and account expiry.

questions.question: Which command lists the users currently logged in to the system?

options.A: df
options.B: uname
options.C: who
options.D: pwd

questions.answer_text: who
questions.explanation: 'who' (and 'w') show logged-in users; 'whoami' shows only your own effective user.

questions.question: Which statement about 'su' and 'sudo' is correct?

options.A: su and sudo behave identically and both log each command to the audit log
options.B: su asks for the user's own password and records every single command that is run as root
options.C: sudo runs a command with elevated rights using the user's own password and logs it
options.D: sudo always opens a permanent root shell that stays open until reboot

questions.answer_text: sudo runs a command with elevated rights using the user's own password and logs it
questions.explanation: sudo gives controlled, logged privilege use with the user's own password; su needs the target user's password.

questions.question: Which system call creates a new child process in UNIX/Linux?

options.A: exit()
options.B: fork()
options.C: exec()
options.D: wait()

questions.answer_text: fork()
questions.explanation: fork() duplicates the calling process; exec() then loads a new program into it.

questions.question: On success, fork() returns:

options.A: -1 to the child and 0 to the parent
options.B: The parent's PID to the child and 0 to the parent
options.C: 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent
options.D: 1 to both processes

questions.answer_text: 0 to the child and the child's PID to the parent
questions.explanation: The return value tells each process who it is; -1 is returned to the parent only if fork fails.

questions.question: The exec() family of system calls:

options.A: Replaces the current process image with a new program
options.B: Creates an exact copy of the current process as a child
options.C: Makes the parent wait until the child process finishes
options.D: Terminates the current process and returns its exit status

questions.answer_text: Replaces the current process image with a new program
questions.explanation: exec keeps the same PID but loads a new program; fork + exec is how shells run commands.

questions.question: A process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not read its exit status is a:

options.A: Zombie process
options.B: Daemon process
options.C: Thread
options.D: Orphan process

questions.answer_text: Zombie process
questions.explanation: Zombies show state 'Z' in ps; the parent must call wait() to reap them.

questions.question: A process whose parent has terminated and which is adopted by init/systemd is called:

options.A: Zombie process
options.B: Child thread
options.C: Orphan process
options.D: Daemon process

questions.answer_text: Orphan process
questions.explanation: Orphans are re-parented to PID 1, which reaps them when they exit.

questions.question: What is the PID of init/systemd, the first user-space process?
questions.explanation: PID 1 is init/systemd; it starts other services and adopts orphan processes.

questions.question: The command 'kill -9 <PID>' sends which signal?

options.A: SIGINT
options.B: SIGHUP
options.C: SIGTERM
options.D: SIGKILL

questions.answer_text: SIGKILL
questions.explanation: 9 = SIGKILL; 15 = SIGTERM (default for kill); 1 = SIGHUP; 2 = SIGINT.

questions.question: Why should 'kill -15' (SIGTERM) be tried before 'kill -9' (SIGKILL) on a database process?

options.A: SIGTERM also kills the parent process and all its siblings
options.B: SIGTERM cannot be caught or ignored, so it always succeeds
options.C: SIGTERM lets the process close files and release locks cleanly
options.D: SIGTERM stops the process faster because it skips all cleanup

questions.answer_text: SIGTERM lets the process close files and release locks cleanly
questions.explanation: SIGKILL stops the process instantly with no cleanup, risking corrupt files, stale locks and orphan shared memory.

questions.question: Which signal can neither be caught nor ignored by a process?

options.A: SIGHUP
options.B: SIGINT
options.C: SIGKILL
options.D: SIGTERM

questions.answer_text: SIGKILL
questions.explanation: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are handled by the kernel directly; programs cannot trap them.

questions.question: Pressing Ctrl+C in a terminal sends which signal to the foreground process?

options.A: SIGTSTP
options.B: SIGKILL
options.C: SIGTERM
options.D: SIGINT

questions.answer_text: SIGINT
questions.explanation: Ctrl+C = SIGINT (interrupt); Ctrl+Z = SIGTSTP (suspend).

questions.question: Which command gives a continuously updating view of running processes with CPU and memory usage?

options.A: ps
options.B: top
options.C: cat
options.D: ls

questions.answer_text: top
questions.explanation: top (or htop) refreshes live; ps gives a one-time snapshot.

questions.question: The 'nice' value range in Linux is:

options.B: -20 to 19, lower value means higher priority
options.C: 0 to 99, higher value means higher priority
options.D: 1 to 20, lower means lower priority

questions.answer_text: -20 to 19, lower value means higher priority
questions.explanation: -20 is the most favourable priority; only root can set negative nice values.

questions.question: Which command lets a job keep running even after the user logs out of the session?

options.A: fg
options.B: nohup
options.C: jobs
options.D: bg

questions.answer_text: nohup
questions.explanation: nohup ignores the hangup signal (SIGHUP) sent at logout; output goes to nohup.out.

questions.question: Swap space in Linux is:

options.A: Read-only memory that holds the BIOS and boot firmware
options.B: A RAM area reserved exclusively for the kernel's own code
options.C: Disk space used as an extension of RAM when physical memory is full
options.D: A reserved part of the CPU cache used for frequently accessed pages

questions.answer_text: Disk space used as an extension of RAM when physical memory is full
questions.explanation: Pages not in active use are moved to swap; heavy swapping slows the system.

questions.question: Thrashing refers to a condition where:

options.A: The system spends more time paging/swapping than executing processes
options.B: The CPU overheats under sustained load and throttles its clock speed
options.C: Two processes keep waiting for each other's resources indefinitely
options.D: The disk becomes so fragmented that file reads slow down badly

questions.answer_text: The system spends more time paging/swapping than executing processes
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the working set does not fit in RAM; adding memory or reducing load fixes it.

questions.question: Which command shows used and free RAM along with swap usage?

options.A: free -h
options.B: du -sh
options.C: lsblk
options.D: df -h

questions.answer_text: free -h
questions.explanation: free shows memory; df shows disk space of file systems; du shows space used by files/directories.

questions.question: The Linux OOM killer:

options.A: Rotates and compresses old log files to free disk space
options.B: Scans memory pages for viruses and malicious code
options.C: Clears the page cache every hour to keep memory free
options.D: Terminates processes when the system runs out of memory

questions.answer_text: Terminates processes when the system runs out of memory
questions.explanation: Out-Of-Memory killer picks a process (based on oom_score) to free memory and keep the kernel alive.

questions.question: A program that keeps allocating memory but never releases it causes a:

options.A: Race condition
options.B: Memory leak
options.C: Deadlock
options.D: Page fault storm only

questions.answer_text: Memory leak
questions.explanation: Memory leaks slowly exhaust RAM and may trigger swapping or the OOM killer.

questions.question: The crontab entry '30 2 * * 1 /opt/backup.sh' runs the script:

options.A: On the 30th of every month at 2 AM
options.B: At 02:30 every day
options.C: At 02:30 every Monday
options.D: Every 30 minutes on 2 January

questions.answer_text: At 02:30 every Monday
questions.explanation: Fields: minute(30) hour(2) day-of-month(*) month(*) day-of-week(1=Monday).

questions.question: What is the correct order of the five time fields in a crontab entry?

options.A: Minute, Hour, Day of month, Month, Day of week
options.B: Hour, Minute, Day of month, Month, Day of week
options.C: Minute, Hour, Month, Day of month, Day of week
options.D: Day of week, Month, Day of month, Hour, Minute

questions.answer_text: Minute, Hour, Day of month, Month, Day of week
questions.explanation: Mnemonic: 'm h dom mon dow'.

questions.question: The cron expression '*/15 * * * *' means:

options.A: At the 15th minute of every hour only
options.B: Every 15 hours
options.C: On the 15th of every month
options.D: Every 15 minutes

questions.answer_text: Every 15 minutes
questions.explanation: '*/15' in the minute field means every 15th minute: 0, 15, 30, 45.

questions.question: Which command opens the current user's crontab for editing?

options.A: crontab -r
options.B: crontab -l
options.C: crontab -e
options.D: cron --edit

questions.answer_text: crontab -e
questions.explanation: -e edits, -l lists, -r removes the crontab (careful: no confirmation).

questions.question: To run a job only once at a specific future time, the most suitable command is:

options.A: at
options.B: cron
options.C: watch
options.D: anacron

questions.answer_text: at
questions.explanation: 'at' schedules one-time jobs; cron is for recurring jobs; anacron for jobs on machines not always on.

questions.question: The first line '#!/bin/bash' in a shell script is called the shebang. It tells the system:

options.A: To make the script executable
options.B: Which interpreter should run the script
options.C: To print the bash version
options.D: That the line is a comment for humans only

questions.answer_text: Which interpreter should run the script
questions.explanation: The kernel reads '#!' and runs the named interpreter; execute permission still has to be set with chmod +x.

questions.question: In a shell script, the special variable $? holds:

options.A: Process ID (PID) of the current shell
options.B: Name of the script that is being executed
options.C: Exit status of the last executed command
options.D: Number of arguments passed to the script

questions.answer_text: Exit status of the last executed command
questions.explanation: $? = last exit status, $$ = PID of shell, $# = number of arguments, $0 = script name.

questions.question: In a shell script, $# represents:

options.A: The exit status of the last command that was run
options.B: The PID of the most recent background job started
options.C: All the arguments joined together as a single string
options.D: The number of positional arguments passed to the script

questions.answer_text: The number of positional arguments passed to the script
questions.explanation: $# counts arguments; $@ and $* expand to the arguments themselves.

questions.question: By convention, an exit status of 0 from a command means:

options.A: Failure
options.B: Success
options.C: Syntax error
options.D: Permission denied

questions.answer_text: Success
questions.explanation: Any non-zero exit code indicates some kind of failure.

questions.question: The pipe operator '|' in Linux:

options.A: Runs the command in the background as a separate job
options.B: Sends the output of one command as input to the next
options.C: Appends the output of a command to an existing file
options.D: Redirects the output of a command into a new file

questions.answer_text: Sends the output of one command as input to the next
questions.explanation: Example: ps -ef | grep oracle. '>' redirects, '>>' appends, '&' runs in background.

questions.question: On systemd-based Linux, which command is used to view system journal logs?

options.A: lastlog
options.B: logrotate
options.C: journalctl
options.D: dmesg

questions.answer_text: journalctl
questions.explanation: journalctl reads logs collected by systemd-journald; e.g. journalctl -u sshd.

questions.question: The 'dmesg' command displays:

options.A: The shell command history of the current user
options.B: Mail messages waiting in the user's local mailbox
options.C: Output and error messages of the cron jobs run by all users on the system
options.D: Kernel ring buffer messages such as boot and driver events

questions.answer_text: Kernel ring buffer messages such as boot and driver events
questions.explanation: dmesg is useful to diagnose hardware, disk and driver problems.

questions.question: The main purpose of 'logrotate' is to:

options.A: Forward all log messages in real time to a central SIEM server for analysis
options.B: Search log files for errors and email the results to admins
options.C: Encrypt log files so that only the root user can read them
options.D: Rotate, compress and delete old logs so the disk does not fill up

questions.answer_text: Rotate, compress and delete old logs so the disk does not fill up
questions.explanation: logrotate runs daily (via cron/systemd timer) based on /etc/logrotate.conf.

questions.question: Syslog messages are sent over the network by default on which port?

options.A: TCP 22
options.B: UDP 161
options.C: UDP 514
options.D: TCP 443

questions.answer_text: UDP 514
questions.explanation: Traditional syslog uses UDP 514; secure syslog over TLS commonly uses TCP 6514.

questions.question: Which command shows new lines being written to a log file in real time?

options.A: head -f /var/log/messages
options.B: less -n /var/log/messages
options.C: tail -f /var/log/messages
options.D: cat -f /var/log/messages

questions.answer_text: tail -f /var/log/messages
questions.explanation: tail -f 'follows' the file as it grows.

questions.question: On RHEL/CentOS, authentication events such as SSH logins and sudo usage are logged in:

options.A: /var/log/maillog
options.B: /var/log/boot.log
options.C: /var/log/cron
options.D: /var/log/secure

questions.answer_text: /var/log/secure
questions.explanation: On Debian/Ubuntu the equivalent file is /var/log/auth.log.

questions.question: Which command is mainly used to monitor disk I/O statistics along with CPU utilisation?

options.A: iostat
options.B: whoami
options.C: uptime
options.D: free

questions.answer_text: iostat
questions.explanation: iostat (sysstat package) reports per-device reads/writes and CPU usage; vmstat and sar are related tools.

questions.question: The three load average figures shown by 'uptime' represent:

options.A: Average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 hours
options.B: Average CPU usage of the first, second and third core
options.C: Number of logged-in users, running processes and threads
options.D: Average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes

questions.answer_text: Average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes
questions.explanation: A load average consistently above the number of CPU cores means processes are waiting.

questions.question: Which command displays the kernel release version?

options.A: whoami
options.B: uptime
options.C: df -h
options.D: uname -r

questions.answer_text: uname -r
questions.explanation: uname -a shows all system info; -r shows kernel release.

questions.question: The relational model of data was proposed by:

options.A: Peter Chen
options.B: E. F. Codd
options.C: Charles Bachman
options.D: Larry Ellison

questions.answer_text: E. F. Codd
questions.explanation: Codd proposed the relational model in 1970; Peter Chen proposed the ER model; Ellison co-founded Oracle.

questions.question: In an RDBMS, data is stored in the form of:

options.A: Network graphs of linked records and pointers
options.B: Hierarchical trees of parent and child records
options.C: Tables (relations) made of rows and columns
options.D: Key-value pairs without any fixed structure

questions.answer_text: Tables (relations) made of rows and columns
questions.explanation: A relation = table; a tuple = row; an attribute = column.

questions.question: The number of rows (tuples) in a relation is called its ____, and the number of columns (attributes) is called its ____.

options.A: Degree, Cardinality
options.B: Schema, Instance
options.C: Domain, Arity
options.D: Cardinality, Degree

questions.answer_text: Cardinality, Degree
questions.explanation: Cardinality counts tuples; degree counts attributes.

questions.question: A candidate key is also called a 'minimal super key' because:

options.A: It is the only key that is allowed to contain NULL values
options.B: No proper subset of it can uniquely identify a row
options.C: It must always consist of exactly one column
options.D: It is always chosen from the smallest table in the schema

questions.answer_text: No proper subset of it can uniquely identify a row
questions.explanation: A super key may have extra columns; a candidate key has none that can be removed while staying unique.

questions.question: A primary key column must be:

options.A: Unique and NOT NULL
options.B: Repeated but NOT NULL
options.C: Always made of two or more columns
options.D: Unique but may be NULL

questions.answer_text: Unique and NOT NULL
questions.explanation: A table can have only one primary key; it enforces entity integrity.

questions.question: A table that has no primary key (allowing duplicate or NULL identifiers) violates which integrity rule?

options.A: Referential integrity
options.B: Domain integrity
options.C: User-defined integrity
options.D: Entity integrity

questions.answer_text: Entity integrity
questions.explanation: Entity integrity: every row must be uniquely identifiable by a non-null primary key.

questions.question: A foreign key is mainly used to enforce:

options.A: Domain integrity
options.B: Referential integrity
options.C: Data encryption
options.D: Entity integrity

questions.answer_text: Referential integrity
questions.explanation: A foreign key value must match a primary/unique key in the parent table or be NULL.

questions.question: Candidate keys that are NOT chosen as the primary key are called:

options.A: Surrogate keys
options.B: Alternate keys
options.C: Super keys
options.D: Foreign keys

questions.answer_text: Alternate keys
questions.explanation: E.g. if Account_No is the PK, a unique PAN column could be an alternate key.

questions.question: With 'ON DELETE CASCADE' defined on a foreign key, deleting a parent row will:

options.A: Automatically delete the matching child rows
options.B: Copy the child rows to an archive table
options.C: Be rejected if child rows exist
options.D: Set the foreign key column of the matching child rows to NULL

questions.answer_text: Automatically delete the matching child rows
questions.explanation: Rejecting is the default (no action); SET NULL is a separate option.

questions.question: A star schema consists of:

options.A: A central fact table linked to denormalised dimension tables
options.B: Dimension tables further normalised into sub-dimension tables
options.C: A single flat table holding all facts and all dimensions
options.D: Only tables normalised to 3NF, linked one after another in a chain

questions.answer_text: A central fact table linked to denormalised dimension tables
questions.explanation: Normalised (split) dimensions form a snowflake schema; star is simpler and faster for reporting.

questions.question: In an ER diagram, a rectangle represents an entity. A diamond represents a:

options.A: Attribute
options.B: Weak entity
options.C: Primary key
options.D: Relationship

questions.answer_text: Relationship
questions.explanation: Ellipse = attribute, double rectangle = weak entity, diamond = relationship.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a DDL command?

options.A: UPDATE
options.B: DROP
options.C: ALTER
options.D: TRUNCATE

questions.answer_text: UPDATE
questions.explanation: UPDATE is DML. DDL defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME.

questions.question: GRANT and REVOKE belong to which category of SQL commands?

options.A: DML
options.B: DDL
options.C: DCL
options.D: TCL

questions.answer_text: DCL
questions.explanation: Data Control Language manages privileges.

questions.question: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT are:

options.A: TCL commands
options.B: DCL commands
options.C: DQL commands
options.D: DDL commands

questions.answer_text: TCL commands
questions.explanation: Transaction Control Language manages transactions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a DML command?

options.A: DROP
options.B: COMMIT
options.C: GRANT
options.D: MERGE

questions.answer_text: MERGE
questions.explanation: DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE (and SELECT in many classifications).

questions.question: TRUNCATE is generally faster than DELETE because:

options.A: It fires the table's DELETE triggers in parallel threads
options.B: It compresses the table first and then removes the rows
options.C: It deallocates data pages instead of logging each row deletion
options.D: It deletes rows in parallel batches of one thousand at a time

questions.answer_text: It deallocates data pages instead of logging each row deletion
questions.explanation: DELETE logs each row (and fires triggers); TRUNCATE is a DDL operation with minimal logging and no WHERE clause.

questions.question: In Oracle, which of the following CANNOT be rolled back with a ROLLBACK statement?

options.A: DELETE FROM table
options.B: TRUNCATE TABLE
options.C: INSERT INTO table
options.D: UPDATE table

questions.answer_text: TRUNCATE TABLE
questions.explanation: DDL statements issue an implicit commit in Oracle, so TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back.

questions.question: What is the difference between DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE TABLE?

options.A: Both can be filtered with a WHERE clause
options.B: Both remove only the data
options.C: TRUNCATE removes structure and data; DROP removes only the data
options.D: DROP removes structure and data; TRUNCATE removes only the data

questions.answer_text: DROP removes structure and data; TRUNCATE removes only the data
questions.explanation: After TRUNCATE the empty table still exists; after DROP it does not.

questions.question: Which query correctly sets the age of the student with ID 101 to 21?

options.A: MODIFY student SET age = 21 WHERE student_id = 101;
options.B: UPDATE student age = 21 WHERE student_id = 101;
options.C: UPDATE student SET age = 21 WHERE student_id = 101;
options.D: UPDATE student SET age = 21, student_id = 101;

questions.answer_text: UPDATE student SET age = 21 WHERE student_id = 101;
questions.explanation: Syntax: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition. Without WHERE every row would be updated.

questions.question: The main difference between WHERE and HAVING is:

options.A: HAVING can be used only in queries that do not contain GROUP BY
options.B: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
options.C: HAVING filters rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups after aggregation
options.D: WHERE works only on numeric columns; HAVING works on any column type

questions.answer_text: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
questions.explanation: Aggregate conditions like COUNT(*) > 5 go in HAVING.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an SQL aggregate function?

options.A: SUM()
options.B: COUNT()
options.C: MAX()
options.D: UPPER()

questions.answer_text: UPPER()
questions.explanation: UPPER is a single-row (scalar) string function.

questions.question: 'SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;' returns:

options.A: Only the first 5 departments along with their employee counts
options.B: Departments that have more than 5 employees, with their counts
options.C: All departments, counting at most 5 employees for each one
options.D: Employees whose department number is greater than 5

questions.answer_text: Departments that have more than 5 employees, with their counts
questions.explanation: GROUP BY forms one group per department; HAVING keeps only groups with more than 5 rows.

questions.question: Table A has 10 rows and table B has 5 rows. How many rows does 'SELECT * FROM A, B;' return?
questions.explanation: Without a join condition the result is a Cartesian product (cross join): 10 x 5 = 50.

questions.question: 'SELECT * FROM R1, R2' without any WHERE condition produces a:

options.A: Left outer join
options.B: Cartesian product (cross join)
options.C: Natural join
options.D: Self join

questions.answer_text: Cartesian product (cross join)
questions.explanation: Every row of R1 is combined with every row of R2.

questions.question: When only the keyword JOIN is written (without INNER/LEFT/RIGHT), the database performs:

options.A: Cross join
options.B: Left outer join
options.C: Inner join
options.D: Full outer join

questions.answer_text: Inner join
questions.explanation: JOIN defaults to INNER JOIN, returning only matching rows.

questions.question: A LEFT OUTER JOIN returns:

options.A: Every possible combination of rows from the left table with rows from the right table
options.B: All rows of the left table plus matching right-table rows, with NULLs where unmatched
options.C: All rows of the right table plus matching left-table rows, with NULLs where unmatched
options.D: Only the rows that have matching values in both the left and the right tables

questions.answer_text: All rows of the left table plus matching right-table rows, with NULLs where unmatched
questions.explanation: RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image; FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both.

questions.question: How does UNION differ from UNION ALL?

options.A: UNION ALL removes duplicate rows; UNION keeps them
options.B: UNION joins columns; UNION ALL joins rows
options.C: There is no difference
options.D: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them

questions.answer_text: UNION removes duplicate rows; UNION ALL keeps them
questions.explanation: UNION ALL is faster because it skips the duplicate-removal sort.

questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates JOIN and UNION?

options.A: JOIN stacks rows of compatible queries; UNION combines columns of related tables
options.B: JOIN needs the same number of columns in each table; UNION does not need it
options.C: JOIN combines columns of related tables; UNION stacks rows of compatible queries
options.D: UNION needs a common key column in both queries; JOIN does not need any key

questions.answer_text: JOIN combines columns of related tables; UNION stacks rows of compatible queries
questions.explanation: UNION needs the same number of columns with compatible data types in each SELECT.

questions.question: Finding each employee's manager name from a single EMP table (emp_id, name, mgr_id) needs a:

options.A: Self join
options.B: UNION
options.C: Natural join with another table
options.D: Cross join

questions.answer_text: Self join
questions.explanation: The table is joined to itself using aliases: e.mgr_id = m.emp_id.

questions.question: A correlated subquery is one that:

options.A: Always returns more than one column to the outer query
options.B: Can be written only in the FROM clause as an inline view
options.C: Runs only once, before the outer query, and passes its single result to it
options.D: Refers to columns of the outer query and runs once for each outer row

questions.answer_text: Refers to columns of the outer query and runs once for each outer row
questions.explanation: Because it is re-evaluated per row, correlated subqueries can be slow on large tables.

questions.question: Which condition correctly finds rows where the 'email' column has no value?

options.A: WHERE email IN (NULL)
options.B: WHERE email IS NULL
options.C: WHERE email == ''
options.D: WHERE email = NULL

questions.answer_text: WHERE email IS NULL
questions.explanation: NULL means unknown; comparison with '=' gives UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

questions.question: A view in SQL is:

options.A: A virtual table defined by a stored query
options.B: An index built on several columns of a table
options.C: A read-only backup of a schema's tables
options.D: A physical copy of a table refreshed nightly

questions.answer_text: A virtual table defined by a stored query
questions.explanation: A normal view stores only the query; a materialized view physically stores the result.

questions.question: A materialized view differs from a normal view because it:

options.A: Cannot be queried directly and is used only by the optimizer
options.B: Always shows real-time data without using any storage at all
options.C: Can be created only on a single table, without any joins
options.D: Physically stores the query result and is refreshed periodically

questions.answer_text: Physically stores the query result and is refreshed periodically
questions.explanation: Materialized views are common in reporting/DWH to pre-compute expensive joins and aggregates.

questions.question: The main purpose of normalization is to:

options.A: Reduce data redundancy and avoid update anomalies
options.B: Add redundancy deliberately so that reports run faster
options.C: Create indexes on every column that is used in queries
options.D: Encrypt sensitive columns such as PAN and Aadhaar

questions.answer_text: Reduce data redundancy and avoid update anomalies
questions.explanation: Anomalies: insertion, update and deletion anomalies caused by duplicated data.

questions.question: A table is in First Normal Form (1NF) when:

options.A: Every column holds atomic values and there are no repeating groups
options.B: Every determinant in the table is a candidate key
options.C: No non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key
options.D: No non-key attribute depends transitively on the primary key

questions.answer_text: Every column holds atomic values and there are no repeating groups
questions.explanation: E.g. a 'phone_numbers' column holding '98xx, 97xx' violates 1NF.

questions.question: A table is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and:

options.A: No non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
options.B: It has no multi-valued dependency
options.C: Every determinant is a super key
options.D: No non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key

questions.answer_text: No non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependency; 3NF removes transitive dependency.

questions.question: A table is in 3NF when it is in 2NF and:

options.A: The table does not reference any other table through foreign keys
options.B: Every column of the table has its own separate index
options.C: There is no transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the key
options.D: The table does not contain any composite primary key at all

questions.answer_text: There is no transitive dependency of non-key attributes on the key
questions.explanation: Example: Emp(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name) - dept_name depends on dept_id, not directly on emp_id.

questions.question: BCNF is often called '3.5 NF' because:

options.A: It is a weaker form of 3NF that permits some transitive dependencies
options.B: It sits halfway between 3NF and 4NF and still allows partial dependencies
options.C: It is simply 3NF applied only to tables that have a single-column key
options.D: It is a stricter form of 3NF requiring every determinant to be a candidate key

questions.answer_text: It is a stricter form of 3NF requiring every determinant to be a candidate key
questions.explanation: Every BCNF table is in 3NF, but not every 3NF table is in BCNF.

questions.question: In table ORDER_ITEM(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name) with composite key (order_id, product_id), product_name depends only on product_id. The table violates:

options.A: 2NF
options.B: BCNF only, but satisfies 3NF
options.C: 1NF
options.D: No normal form

questions.answer_text: 2NF
questions.explanation: A non-key attribute depending on part of a composite key is a partial dependency, which breaks 2NF.

questions.question: Denormalization means:

options.A: Removing all indexes to speed up inserts and updates
options.B: Splitting large tables further into higher normal forms such as BCNF and 4NF
options.C: Adding controlled redundancy to improve read/report performance
options.D: Deleting duplicate rows to clean up a table's data

questions.answer_text: Adding controlled redundancy to improve read/report performance
questions.explanation: Common in data warehouses where fast reads matter more than update efficiency.

questions.question: The main benefit of creating an index on a column is:

options.A: Faster data retrieval for queries filtering or sorting on that column
options.B: Faster INSERT and UPDATE operations on that table, since rows are kept pre-sorted
options.C: Automatic encryption of all values stored in that column
options.D: Lower storage usage because the table's data gets compressed

questions.answer_text: Faster data retrieval for queries filtering or sorting on that column
questions.explanation: Indexes cost extra storage and slow down writes.

questions.question: Indexing every column of a busy OLTP table is a poor strategy mainly because:

options.A: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update all the indexes, slowing writes
options.B: Indexes make SELECT queries slower because more data must be read each time
options.C: Most databases allow only one index to be created on each table
options.D: Indexes automatically delete duplicate rows, causing loss of data

questions.answer_text: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update all the indexes, slowing writes
questions.explanation: Too many indexes also consume storage and confuse the optimizer; index only columns used in searches/joins.

questions.question: A bitmap index is most suitable for:

options.A: Columns that are updated thousands of times every second
options.B: Low-cardinality columns like gender or status in a data warehouse
options.C: Large free-text columns such as customer remarks
options.D: Unique, high-cardinality columns like account number in OLTP

questions.answer_text: Low-cardinality columns like gender or status in a data warehouse
questions.explanation: Bitmap indexes lock badly under heavy concurrent DML, so they suit read-mostly DWH tables.

questions.question: The default index type created in Oracle is:

options.A: B-tree index
options.B: Bitmap index
options.C: Full-text index
options.D: Hash index

questions.answer_text: B-tree index
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX creates a balanced-tree (B-tree) index unless specified otherwise.

questions.question: In SQL Server, a clustered index:

options.A: Stores only pointers to the rows in a separate structure and never the data itself
options.B: Can be created any number of times on the same table
options.C: Decides the physical order of rows, so a table can have only one
options.D: Can be created only on the text columns of a table

questions.answer_text: Decides the physical order of rows, so a table can have only one
questions.explanation: Non-clustered indexes are separate structures pointing to the rows; many are allowed.

questions.question: A query uses 'WHERE UPPER(cust_name) = 'RAVI'' on a column with a normal B-tree index. What usually happens and what is the fix?

options.A: The table gets locked, so a bitmap index should be added instead
options.B: The query fails with an error, so UPPER must be removed from it
options.C: The index is still used normally, so no change to the query or the index is needed
options.D: The index is ignored; create a function-based index on UPPER(cust_name)

questions.answer_text: The index is ignored; create a function-based index on UPPER(cust_name)
questions.explanation: Applying a function to an indexed column prevents normal index use; function-based indexes solve this.

questions.question: The ACID property that ensures 'all or nothing' execution of a transaction is:

options.A: Isolation
options.B: Atomicity
options.C: Durability
options.D: Consistency

questions.answer_text: Atomicity
questions.explanation: If any step fails, all steps of the transaction are undone.

questions.question: ₹20 is debited from account X, but the system crashes before crediting account Y. On restart the database undoes the debit. Which property is being enforced?

options.A: Atomicity
options.B: Durability
options.C: Isolation
options.D: Consistency only

questions.answer_text: Atomicity
questions.explanation: A partial transaction must never remain; it is rolled back as a whole.

questions.question: Which ACID property guarantees that once a transaction is committed, its changes survive a power failure?

options.A: Consistency
options.B: Atomicity
options.C: Durability
options.D: Isolation

questions.answer_text: Durability
questions.explanation: Durability is achieved using redo logs / write-ahead logging flushed to disk at commit.

questions.question: Match the ACID properties with their meaning: (P) Atomicity (Q) Consistency (R) Isolation (S) Durability | (1) Concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work (2) Committed data is permanent (3) All steps or none (4) Database moves from one valid state to another
questions.explanation: Atomicity=all or none, Consistency=valid states, Isolation=no interference, Durability=permanence.

questions.question: Arrange the steps of transferring ₹20 from account X to account Y in the correct order: (1) Read balance of X (2) Write X = X - 20 (3) Read balance of Y (4) Write Y = Y + 20 (5) COMMIT
questions.explanation: Commit comes only after both debit and credit are written, so a failure before commit can roll back both.

questions.question: A 'dirty read' occurs when a transaction:

options.A: Reads data from a disk block that has been physically corrupted
options.B: Sees new rows appear when it repeats the same range query
options.C: Reads the same row twice and gets two different committed values
options.D: Reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed

questions.answer_text: Reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed
questions.explanation: If the other transaction rolls back, the reader has used data that never officially existed.

questions.question: Which isolation level prevents dirty reads but still allows non-repeatable reads?

options.A: REPEATABLE READ
options.B: SERIALIZABLE
options.C: READ COMMITTED
options.D: READ UNCOMMITTED

questions.answer_text: READ COMMITTED
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED is Oracle's default; REPEATABLE READ prevents non-repeatable reads; SERIALIZABLE prevents phantoms too.

questions.question: A 'phantom read' happens when:

options.A: Two transactions read the same value and one overwrites the other's update
options.B: A repeated range query returns new rows inserted and committed by another transaction
options.C: A transaction reads data that another transaction has changed but not yet committed
options.D: A deadlock is resolved by rolling back the transaction that started last

questions.answer_text: A repeated range query returns new rows inserted and committed by another transaction
questions.explanation: Phantoms are prevented only at the SERIALIZABLE level (or by range locks).

questions.question: Which statement about shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks is correct?

options.A: An X lock on a row can be shared with S locks held by other reading transactions
options.B: Many transactions can hold S locks on a row together, but an X lock allows no other lock
options.C: An S lock must be obtained before a transaction is allowed to update a row
options.D: Many transactions can hold X locks on the same row as long as they only read it

questions.answer_text: Many transactions can hold S locks on a row together, but an X lock allows no other lock
questions.explanation: S = read lock (compatible with other S); X = write lock (incompatible with everything).

questions.question: Transaction T1 holds a shared lock on a row. Transaction T2 now requests an exclusive lock on the same row. What happens?

options.A: T1 is aborted automatically
options.B: Both get exclusive locks
options.C: T2 waits until T1 releases its lock
options.D: T2 gets the lock immediately, since locks are row-level

questions.answer_text: T2 waits until T1 releases its lock
questions.explanation: S and X are incompatible, so the requester waits (or times out).

questions.question: In a DBMS, a deadlock is a situation where:

options.A: The transaction log becomes full and stops all writes
options.B: A transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet been committed
options.C: A table is created without any primary key constraint
options.D: Two or more transactions each wait for a lock held by the other

questions.answer_text: Two or more transactions each wait for a lock held by the other
questions.explanation: Example: T1 locks A and wants B; T2 locks B and wants A.

questions.question: When Oracle detects a deadlock between two sessions, it:

options.A: Restarts the database instance to clear all the locks
options.B: Rolls back the statement of one session and raises ORA-00060
options.C: Waits indefinitely until a DBA manually kills one session
options.D: Kills both sessions and rolls back both transactions fully

questions.answer_text: Rolls back the statement of one session and raises ORA-00060
questions.explanation: Oracle detects deadlocks automatically; the application must handle ORA-00060 and retry.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four necessary (Coffman) conditions for deadlock?

options.A: Mutual exclusion
options.B: Hold and wait
options.C: Preemption of resources
options.D: Circular wait

questions.answer_text: Preemption of resources
questions.explanation: The fourth condition is 'No preemption'. Allowing preemption breaks deadlock.

questions.question: In two-phase locking (2PL), a transaction:

options.A: Locks only two rows at a time and releases both before it locks any further rows
options.B: Takes all of its locks in the first phase and then commits in the second phase without ever releasing them
options.C: Uses only shared locks in the first phase and only exclusive locks in the second
options.D: Acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring after releasing

questions.answer_text: Acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring after releasing
questions.explanation: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability; strict 2PL holds X locks until commit.

questions.question: Two tellers read balance ₹1000 at the same time; one adds ₹100 and the other subtracts ₹50; the final balance shows ₹950. This is the:

options.A: Lost update problem
options.B: Phantom read problem
options.C: Deadlock problem
options.D: Dirty read problem

questions.answer_text: Lost update problem
questions.explanation: The second write overwrote the first. Proper locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) prevents it.

questions.question: In Oracle, readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers because Oracle uses:

options.A: Dirty reads allowed by default for all sessions
options.B: Multi-version read consistency using undo data
options.C: Bitmap indexes created automatically on all tables
options.D: Table-level locks taken for every query

questions.answer_text: Multi-version read consistency using undo data
questions.explanation: A query sees a consistent snapshot rebuilt from undo, as of the time it started (MVCC).

questions.question: Stored procedures are generally safer and faster than sending raw SQL from application code because they:

options.A: Always run on a separate server, so they never add load to the database server
options.B: Are pre-compiled, cut network round-trips and use parameters that resist SQL injection
options.C: Run without any privilege checks, so they avoid permission overhead on each call
options.D: Bypass the transaction log, so they write data faster than normal SQL statements

questions.answer_text: Are pre-compiled, cut network round-trips and use parameters that resist SQL injection
questions.explanation: Users can be given EXECUTE on the procedure without direct table access, supporting least privilege.

questions.question: A database trigger is:

options.A: A user account with DBA rights that is used to run maintenance tasks
options.B: Code that runs automatically when a specified event like INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE occurs
options.C: A scheduled job that backs up a table at a fixed time every day
options.D: A special type of index that is maintained automatically to speed up INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements

questions.answer_text: Code that runs automatically when a specified event like INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE occurs
questions.explanation: Triggers are used for auditing, enforcing complex rules and deriving column values.

questions.question: Standard DML triggers can be defined to fire on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Which statement cannot fire a DML trigger?

options.A: INSERT
options.B: UPDATE
options.C: DELETE
options.D: SELECT

questions.answer_text: SELECT
questions.explanation: A plain SELECT does not change data, so there is no DML trigger for it.

questions.question: The 'FOR EACH ROW' clause in an Oracle trigger makes it:

options.A: A trigger that fires only on SELECT
options.B: A statement-level trigger that fires once per statement
options.C: A trigger that can never be disabled
options.D: A row-level trigger that fires once for every affected row

questions.answer_text: A row-level trigger that fires once for every affected row
questions.explanation: Without FOR EACH ROW, the trigger fires once per statement regardless of rows affected.

questions.question: In an Oracle row-level UPDATE trigger, :OLD and :NEW refer to:

options.A: The old and new user sessions
options.B: The old and new table names
options.C: Column values before and after the update
options.D: The previous and next row in the table

questions.answer_text: Column values before and after the update
questions.explanation: For INSERT only :NEW is meaningful; for DELETE only :OLD.

questions.question: In PL/SQL, a FUNCTION differs from a PROCEDURE mainly because a function:

options.A: Runs only once each time the database instance is started
options.B: Cannot contain SQL statements, only procedural PL/SQL logic
options.C: Cannot accept any parameters from the calling program
options.D: Must return a value and can be called inside a SQL statement

questions.answer_text: Must return a value and can be called inside a SQL statement
questions.explanation: Procedures may return values through OUT parameters but are called as standalone statements.

questions.question: A cursor in PL/SQL is used to:

options.A: Process the rows returned by a query one at a time
options.B: Lock the entire database while a query is running
options.C: Encrypt the result set returned by a query
options.D: Create a backup copy of a table before an update

questions.answer_text: Process the rows returned by a query one at a time
questions.explanation: Implicit cursors are created for single DML; explicit cursors are declared for multi-row queries.

questions.question: An Oracle 'hot backup' is a backup taken:

options.A: After a clean shutdown of the database; it needs NOARCHIVELOG mode
options.B: Only during the month-end batch, when no users are logged in
options.C: While the database is open and in use; it needs ARCHIVELOG mode
options.D: Only of the control file and parameter file, while the database is open

questions.answer_text: While the database is open and in use; it needs ARCHIVELOG mode
questions.explanation: Archived redo logs are needed to make the online backup consistent during recovery.

questions.question: A 'cold backup' of an Oracle database is taken:

options.A: After the database is shut down cleanly
options.B: Using only the export utility
options.C: While users are running transactions
options.D: Every second automatically

questions.answer_text: After the database is shut down cleanly
questions.explanation: Cold (offline) backups are consistent but need downtime.

questions.question: Oracle's built-in tool for physical backup, restore and recovery is:

options.A: SQL*Loader
options.B: RMAN (Recovery Manager)
options.C: TKPROF
options.D: Data Guard Broker

questions.answer_text: RMAN (Recovery Manager)
questions.explanation: RMAN supports full/incremental backups, block-level recovery and backup validation.

questions.question: Oracle Data Pump (expdp / impdp) is mainly used for:

options.A: Mirroring data files between two storage arrays
options.B: Shipping redo logs to the standby database at the DR site in real time
options.C: Monitoring wait events and tuning slow queries
options.D: Logical export and import of schemas, tables and data

questions.answer_text: Logical export and import of schemas, tables and data
questions.explanation: Data Pump creates logical dump files; RMAN takes physical backups.

questions.question: To recover an Oracle database to 11:00 AM yesterday (point-in-time recovery), you need:

options.A: A backup taken before 11:00 AM plus all archived redo logs up to that time
options.B: Only today's online redo log files from the current log group
options.C: Only the current control file and the server parameter file
options.D: Only the latest export dump file, taken after 11:00 AM today, plus the current control file

questions.answer_text: A backup taken before 11:00 AM plus all archived redo logs up to that time
questions.explanation: Restore the backup, then roll forward using archived logs until the target time/SCN.

questions.question: Oracle redo log files record:

options.A: Optimizer statistics gathered for each table and index by the scheduled job
options.B: User passwords along with their expiry dates
options.C: All changes made to the database, used for recovery
options.D: Only the SELECT statements executed by users

questions.answer_text: All changes made to the database, used for recovery
questions.explanation: Redo is replayed to re-apply committed changes after a failure.

questions.question: Oracle UNDO data is used for all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Re-applying committed changes after media failure
options.B: Supporting flashback queries to view data at a past time
options.C: Rolling back transactions that have not been committed
options.D: Providing read-consistent results to long-running queries

questions.answer_text: Re-applying committed changes after media failure
questions.explanation: Re-applying changes (roll forward) is done using redo, not undo.

questions.question: In SQL Server, which backup type contains only the changes made since the last FULL backup?

options.A: Tail-log backup
options.B: Copy-only backup
options.C: Transaction log backup
options.D: Differential backup

questions.answer_text: Differential backup
questions.explanation: Log backups capture changes since the last log backup and allow point-in-time restore.

questions.question: A SQL Server database in FULL recovery model stops processing with a 'transaction log full' error. The most common cause is:

options.A: The tables have too many non-clustered indexes
options.B: Optimizer statistics on large tables are out of date
options.C: Regular transaction log backups are not being taken
options.D: Full database backups are being taken too frequently

questions.answer_text: Regular transaction log backups are not being taken
questions.explanation: In FULL recovery, log space is reused only after a log backup (or if a long open transaction holds it).

questions.question: With Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), the database guarantees that:

options.A: Changed data pages are written to disk before the log records describing them
options.B: Log records describing a change are written to disk before the changed data pages
options.C: Log records are written to disk only when the database is shut down cleanly
options.D: Each query writes its own separate log file, which is deleted after commit

questions.answer_text: Log records describing a change are written to disk before the changed data pages
questions.explanation: After a crash, committed changes are redone and uncommitted ones undone using the log.

questions.question: A database checkpoint:

options.A: Writes modified (dirty) buffers to the data files, shortening crash recovery
options.B: Validates user passwords against the profile's password policy
options.C: Deletes the old archived redo logs that are no longer needed for instance or media recovery
options.D: Starts a new transaction and assigns it a new system change number

questions.answer_text: Writes modified (dirty) buffers to the data files, shortening crash recovery
questions.explanation: Recovery only needs to apply log records after the last checkpoint.

questions.question: The Oracle control file contains:

options.A: Password hashes of all database users along with their granted roles
options.B: The SQL text and execution plans of all recently executed queries
options.C: Database name, locations of data files and redo logs, and checkpoint/SCN information
options.D: All table and index data blocks of the database, stored in compressed form for faster recovery

questions.answer_text: Database name, locations of data files and redo logs, and checkpoint/SCN information
questions.explanation: The database cannot be mounted without a valid control file, so it is usually multiplexed.

questions.question: Which memory area in Oracle is shared by all server and background processes?

options.A: Sort area of each session
options.B: SGA (System Global Area)
options.C: UGA only
options.D: PGA (Program Global Area)

questions.answer_text: SGA (System Global Area)
questions.explanation: SGA includes the buffer cache, shared pool and redo log buffer; PGA is private to each process.

questions.question: In Oracle terminology, an 'instance' consists of:

options.A: Only user schemas
options.B: Only the listener
options.C: Memory structures (SGA) and background processes
options.D: Data files, online redo log files and control files stored on disk

questions.answer_text: Memory structures (SGA) and background processes
questions.explanation: The database is the set of physical files; the instance is what accesses them.

questions.question: The default port of the Oracle TNS listener is:
questions.explanation: 1433 = SQL Server, 3306 = MySQL, 5432 = PostgreSQL.

questions.question: In Oracle Shared Server configuration:

options.A: The database can be opened only in read-only mode for reporting users
options.B: Each user session gets its own dedicated server process for its lifetime
options.C: Two separate databases share the same set of data files and redo logs
options.D: Many user sessions share a small pool of server processes through dispatchers

questions.answer_text: Many user sessions share a small pool of server processes through dispatchers
questions.explanation: Shared server saves memory when there are many mostly idle connections; dedicated server is the default.

questions.question: What is the correct order of OSI layers from bottom (Layer 1) to top (Layer 7)?

options.A: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
options.B: Physical, Network, Data Link, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
options.C: Data Link, Physical, Network, Transport, Session, Application, Presentation
options.D: Physical, Data Link, Transport, Network, Presentation, Session, Application

questions.answer_text: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application
questions.explanation: Mnemonic (bottom-up): 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away'.

questions.question: Routing of packets between different networks happens at which OSI layer?

options.A: Session layer (Layer 5)
options.B: Network layer (Layer 3)
options.C: Transport layer (Layer 4)
options.D: Data Link layer (Layer 2)

questions.answer_text: Network layer (Layer 3)
questions.explanation: Routers use logical (IP) addresses at Layer 3.

questions.question: HTTP, FTP, SMTP and DNS operate at which OSI layer?

options.A: Transport layer (Layer 4)
options.B: Presentation layer (Layer 6)
options.C: Network layer (Layer 3)
options.D: Application layer (Layer 7)

questions.answer_text: Application layer (Layer 7)
questions.explanation: These are application protocols used directly by user programs.

questions.question: The Presentation layer is called the 'data translator' because it:

options.A: Assigns port numbers to sending and receiving applications
options.B: Converts bits into electrical or optical signals
options.C: Finds the best path for packets between networks
options.D: Handles data format conversion, encryption and compression

questions.answer_text: Handles data format conversion, encryption and compression
questions.explanation: It converts data between application format and network format (e.g. ASCII/EBCDIC, encryption/decryption).

questions.question: Which OSI layer establishes, maintains and terminates dialogues between applications, including checkpointing?

options.A: Network layer
options.B: Session layer
options.C: Transport layer
options.D: Presentation layer

questions.answer_text: Session layer
questions.explanation: Session layer provides dialog control and synchronisation points.

questions.question: Error detection using CRC/Frame Check Sequence and physical (MAC) addressing are functions of the:

options.A: Physical layer
options.B: Data Link layer
options.C: Network layer
options.D: Transport layer

questions.answer_text: Data Link layer
questions.explanation: Data Link has two sub-layers: LLC (Logical Link Control) and MAC (Media Access Control).

questions.question: Which layer provides end-to-end delivery, port numbers, segmentation and flow control?

options.A: Session layer
options.B: Network layer
options.C: Transport layer
options.D: Data Link layer

questions.answer_text: Transport layer
questions.explanation: TCP and UDP are Transport layer protocols.

questions.question: A hub works at which OSI layer?

options.A: Physical layer
options.B: Data Link layer
options.C: Transport layer
options.D: Network layer

questions.answer_text: Physical layer
questions.explanation: Hubs/repeaters just regenerate bits; switches are Layer 2; routers are Layer 3.

questions.question: A traditional (Layer 2) switch forwards frames based on:

options.A: IP addresses
options.B: MAC addresses
options.C: Port numbers
options.D: URLs

questions.answer_text: MAC addresses
questions.explanation: The switch keeps a MAC address table (CAM table) mapping MACs to switch ports.

questions.question: Which device is typically used to connect a LAN to a WAN?

options.A: Hub
options.B: Repeater
options.C: Router
options.D: Layer 2 switch

questions.answer_text: Router
questions.explanation: Routers connect different networks and forward traffic between them.

questions.question: Match the OSI layer with its PDU (Protocol Data Unit): (P) Transport (Q) Network (R) Data Link (S) Physical | (1) Frame (2) Bits (3) Segment (4) Packet
questions.explanation: Segment (L4) -> Packet (L3) -> Frame (L2) -> Bits (L1).

questions.question: Network engineers prefer the OSI model as the reference for troubleshooting mainly because:

options.A: It is the protocol stack actually implemented by all hosts on the Internet
options.B: It defines the exact cables and connectors used in every network
options.C: It has fewer layers than TCP/IP, so troubleshooting finishes quicker
options.D: Its seven separate layers allow step-by-step (e.g. bottom-up) isolation of faults

questions.answer_text: Its seven separate layers allow step-by-step (e.g. bottom-up) isolation of faults
questions.explanation: TCP/IP is the implemented stack; OSI's finer separation of functions makes it a better diagnostic framework.

questions.question: SSL/TLS is usually placed between which layers when mapped to the OSI model?

options.A: Between the Transport and Application layers (Session/Presentation)
options.B: Between the Physical and Data Link layers (inside the NIC)
options.C: Between the Data Link and Network layers, working alongside ARP on the LAN
options.D: Inside the Network layer, as a replacement for IP

questions.answer_text: Between the Transport and Application layers (Session/Presentation)
questions.explanation: TLS runs on top of TCP and below application protocols like HTTP (HTTPS).

questions.question: A sniffing attack that captures frames on a shared network segment and an ARP-based man-in-the-middle attack mainly target which OSI layer?

options.A: Presentation layer
options.B: Application layer
options.C: Data Link layer
options.D: Session layer

questions.answer_text: Data Link layer
questions.explanation: ARP poisoning manipulates IP-to-MAC mapping, a Layer 2 weakness.

questions.question: Which is the top layer of the TCP/IP model?

options.A: Transport layer
options.B: Session layer
options.C: Application layer
options.D: Internet layer

questions.answer_text: Application layer
questions.explanation: TCP/IP (4-layer): Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.

questions.question: The Session, Presentation and Application layers of OSI map to which layer of the TCP/IP model?

options.A: Application layer
options.B: Network Access layer
options.C: Transport layer
options.D: Internet layer

questions.answer_text: Application layer
questions.explanation: TCP/IP merges the top three OSI layers into one Application layer.

questions.question: The Physical and Data Link layers of OSI correspond to which TCP/IP layer?

options.A: Host-to-Host (Transport) layer
options.B: Process (Application) layer
options.C: Internet (Network) layer
options.D: Network Access (Link) layer

questions.answer_text: Network Access (Link) layer
questions.explanation: The Internet layer of TCP/IP maps to the OSI Network layer.

questions.question: IP, ICMP and ARP are commonly associated with which layer of the TCP/IP model?

options.A: Application layer
options.B: Transport layer
options.C: Internet layer
options.D: Presentation layer

questions.answer_text: Internet layer
questions.explanation: ARP is sometimes placed between Link and Internet layers, but it is grouped with Internet-layer protocols.

questions.question: How is a TCP connection established?

options.A: FIN, ACK, SYN
options.B: ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
options.C: SYN, ACK, FIN
options.D: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK

questions.answer_text: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
questions.explanation: This is the three-way handshake; the client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client confirms with ACK.

questions.question: A server shows thousands of connections in SYN_RECV state and stops accepting new users. The most likely cause is:

options.A: A UDP broadcast storm saturating the local network
options.B: A SYN flood attack leaving many half-open connections
options.C: Too many completed TCP sessions in ESTABLISHED state
options.D: A DNS misconfiguration preventing name resolution

questions.answer_text: A SYN flood attack leaving many half-open connections
questions.explanation: The server sent SYN-ACK and waits for ACKs that never come; SYN cookies and rate limiting help mitigate.

questions.question: A normal TCP connection is closed using:

options.A: A single RST segment sent by the client
options.B: A three-way exchange of SYN segments
options.C: An ICMP echo request followed by an echo reply
options.D: A four-way exchange of FIN and ACK segments

questions.answer_text: A four-way exchange of FIN and ACK segments
questions.explanation: Each side sends FIN and acknowledges the other's FIN; RST is an abrupt reset.

questions.question: UDP is considered unreliable because it:

options.A: Uses a three-way handshake that often times out
options.B: Works only on wireless networks with high error rates
options.C: Does not guarantee delivery, order or retransmission
options.D: Encrypts all data, which makes it slow and lossy

questions.answer_text: Does not guarantee delivery, order or retransmission
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless with no acknowledgements; reliability, if needed, is left to the application.

questions.question: Core banking transactions prefer TCP over UDP mainly because TCP provides:

options.A: Broadcast capability to send one message to all branches at once
options.B: Guaranteed, ordered delivery with acknowledgements and retransmission
options.C: Built-in encryption of all transaction data without needing TLS
options.D: Lower header overhead and no connection setup, so it is faster

questions.answer_text: Guaranteed, ordered delivery with acknowledgements and retransmission
questions.explanation: Financial data cannot tolerate loss or reordering; UDP is faster but suits voice/video/DNS.

questions.question: Which application is best suited to UDP rather than TCP?

options.A: Sending email using SMTP
options.B: File transfer using FTP
options.C: Internet banking login and fund transfer
options.D: Live video streaming / VoIP

questions.answer_text: Live video streaming / VoIP
questions.explanation: Real-time media prefers speed over retransmission of lost packets.

questions.question: The minimum size of a TCP header and of a UDP header is respectively:

options.A: 40 bytes and 20 bytes
options.B: 20 bytes and 8 bytes
options.C: 20 bytes and 20 bytes
options.D: 8 bytes and 20 bytes

questions.answer_text: 20 bytes and 8 bytes
questions.explanation: Smaller header and no handshake make UDP lighter.

questions.question: TCP flow control, which stops a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver, is achieved using:

options.A: Checksum
options.B: Sliding window
options.C: Time To Live
options.D: Urgent pointer

questions.answer_text: Sliding window
questions.explanation: The receiver advertises a window size telling the sender how much data it can accept.

questions.question: The 'ping' utility uses which protocol?

options.A: TCP
options.B: ICMP
options.C: ARP
options.D: UDP

questions.answer_text: ICMP
questions.explanation: Ping sends ICMP Echo Request (type 8) and expects Echo Reply (type 0).

questions.question: ICMP is vital for network operation even though it carries no user data because it:

options.A: Resolves domain names into IP addresses for client applications
options.B: Encrypts routing updates exchanged between neighbouring routers
options.C: Reports errors and diagnostics such as unreachable hosts and TTL expiry
options.D: Assigns IP addresses automatically to hosts that join the network

questions.answer_text: Reports errors and diagnostics such as unreachable hosts and TTL expiry
questions.explanation: Messages like Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded help routing and tools like ping/traceroute.

questions.question: Traceroute discovers each hop on the path by:

options.A: Sending packets with increasing TTL and reading ICMP Time Exceeded replies
options.B: Opening a TCP session with each router and reading its routing table
options.C: Sending ARP requests to every router and recording their MAC replies
options.D: Querying DNS for the name and address of each router on the path

questions.answer_text: Sending packets with increasing TTL and reading ICMP Time Exceeded replies
questions.explanation: Each router decrements TTL; when it reaches 0 the router replies with ICMP type 11.

questions.question: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) is used to:

options.A: Find the IP address for a given domain name such as www.bank.in
options.B: Find the MAC address for a known IP address
options.C: Assign IP addresses dynamically
options.D: Find the route to a remote network

questions.answer_text: Find the MAC address for a known IP address
questions.explanation: DNS resolves names to IPs; DHCP assigns IPs; ARP resolves IP to MAC on the local network.
